UTLT.ai / team03

The problem

We use water every day, but rarely see how much we use in the moment.

01

Invisible usage

No immediate picture of litres used.

02

Hidden patterns

Repeated habits are easy to miss.

03

Delayed feedback

A bill arrives long after the water flows.

UTLT.ai begins with a simple idea: make consumption visible.

UTLT.ai / problem04

Research

Why we started with water

We used Hyderabad’s groundwater assessment to frame the problem, then focused on what a household can measure.

What we read

The Central Ground Water Board’s 2024 Telangana assessment gave us the local context.

What was missing

Regional data cannot tell a family what happened at its tap. A bill arrives after the water has been used.

What we built around

A live litre count, a daily goal and a check for water that keeps running.

Next test the readings and alert wording with households.

2024 Telangana assessment

Our mission

while they can still act on it.

MEASURE

LEARN

IMPROVE

UTLT.ai / mission05

Interface design

Show the litres first

Hrishi drew the light and dark mobile layouts in Figma. The team turned them into the phone web app.

Build

Keep today’s litres and goal up front. Put the weekly chart and the by-time view a tap away.

Problem

People could mistake the activity pie chart for something the flow meter measured directly.

What we changed

Separate the by-time and activity views. Keep unconfirmed use in Misc. Label demo breakdowns as examples.

Next test the charts and labels with families on different phone sizes.

Team project record

Our solution

UTLT.ai combines a flow sensor, a microcontroller and a phone app.

People can see how much water passed through the sensor, compare days and choose a realistic goal.

How it works

From the meter to the phone over Bluetooth.

01

Sense

The meter produces electrical pulses as water moves.

02

Process

The ESP32 sends pulse counts. The phone converts the difference into estimated litres.

03

Display

The phone shows usage, trends and the goal.

UTLT.ai / how it works08

Model training

Two models, two jobs

The team generated seven-day water-use records for 1,000 simulated households.

Activity suggestions

Train a 36-tree random forest on 800 homes with 200 homes held out. Use volume, time, duration and survey answers.

On-phone questions

Niro runs Hugging Face’s SmolLM2 135M locally. Our LoRA-tuned Qwen model was an earlier experiment.

Where it can go wrong

A single meter cannot name the activity. Ask the household to confirm labels and calculate totals in JavaScript.

96.78% accuracy on synthetic activity sessions. Next validate the household feedback and forecasts on real homes.

Activity model results · Qwen experiment · Live Niro base model

Niro · Live water app

Set a goal. Learn from a week.

Niro is the only place that asks household setup questions. A 137 MB model download opens setup and chat.

Starting goal

Ask about the household, bathing, laundry and other routines. Use a known water total when available. Review and edit the proposed daily goal.

Label a spike

During the first seven days, Niro can highlight an hour. Answer “showering and cooking” or “I don’t remember.” Mixed activities keep one measured total.

Forecast usage

When the week ends, use the median and range of at least three recorded days. Confirmed activity examples help Niro explain similar intervals.

Goal arithmetic and forecasts use app code. Chat runs on the device and clears on reload.

Prototype troubleshooting

01

Signal levels

The sensor and ESP32 require compatible voltage levels.

02

Connections

Loose jumper contacts can look like a sensor fault.

03

Water flow

Air pockets and pump power change the test flow.

04

App pairing

BLE works in the tested setup; device A014 needed wiring fixes.

05

3D printing

The first enclosure print failed. We revised the case and mounted the flow meter and electronics inside.

UTLT.ai / progress12

Proposed gas module

Meter piped gas

An inline gas meter records how many cubic metres pass through the pipe.

Meter and ESP32

The ESP32 reads the meter’s approved pulse or digital output. UTLT.ai shows measured cubic metres and a daily history.

How we’d verify it

Replay a recorded meter signal and compare the app’s daily total with the meter register.

The gas utility or qualified installer handles pipework. A certified gas alarm handles leak detection.

Gas meter pulse output13

Proposed electricity module

Read electricity at the panel

A certified AC meter would measure active power and cumulative energy from the circuit.

Household design

A qualified electrician installs the meter. The ESP32 reads watts and kWh through an isolated digital interface, such as Modbus.

Optional bench test

A 5 V fan and INA219 could validate DC readings and Bluetooth transfer. The report budgets ₹850–₹1,100 for the bench test.

Indicative 17 Nov 2026 estimate, reusing the ESP32. Household AC equipment and installation are separate.

Example for the bench: 5 V × 0.20 A = 1 W. At that power for two hours, the energy used is 2 Wh.

AC meter reference · INA219 reference14

Proposed system architecture

One app for three utilities

Keep the working Bluetooth water demo. A future local gateway would combine readings from all three meters.

Measure

Water meter in litres, piped gas meter in m³, and electricity meter in watts and kWh.

Validate and store

Record the meter, time, unit and quality. Check for gaps and duplicates before calculating daily totals.

Show and share

Give the AI read-only access to checked totals, comparisons and forecasts. Share only supported states with consent.

If a device goes offline, show when it last sent data and leave gaps visible.

UTLT.ai / Proposed system architecture15

AI roadmap

Answers you can check against the meter

Start with water. Compare use at the same time of day, then show the reading and the comparison beside the answer.

Calculate

Use comparable days to learn a home’s usual use. Show a forecast range and leave out comparisons when readings are missing.

Explain

The assistant shows what changed, links to the chart and suggests one check. Users can correct guesses and alerts.

Keep control local

Utility history stays on the home’s devices by default. The pilot is read-only. The household decides what to share.

Sample answer · You’ve used 240 L by 4 pm. On past days you typically used another 160 L by 8 pm. That gives an estimate of 400 L.

UTLT.ai / Proposed AI framework16

Proposed smart-home integration

One test device in both home apps

Use Matter over Wi-Fi. Start with a real enclosure contact switch and verify the state on two platforms.

Google Home

Pair through a compatible hub and check open, closed and restart recovery. Then check which utility states and automations each app supports.

Apple Home

Open a new Matter pairing window and add the same device from iPhone. Remove one home and check that the other still updates.

UTLT.ai keeps the full meter history. Google Home and Apple Home would show supported device states.

Google Home support · Apple Home support17

Future roadmap

What we’d prove before a household pilot

Start with water. Add each new meter and upgrade the AI only after a test shows it helps.

01 · Trust the readings

Compare litres with known volumes. Test dropouts, restarts and duplicates, then link answers back to the meter.

02 · Compare the models

Test on homes we held out. Compare forecast error and false alerts against a simple baseline before expanding the pilot.

03 · Add approved meters

Verify gas and electricity at the register. Test one Matter sensor in both home apps before adding supported states.

Measure any savings against comparable periods. Report litres, cubic metres and kWh separately.
